Project Report

Financial Distress Early-Warning System

A Small-Sample Proof of Concept for Explainable Corporate Risk Analytics

A simple, easy-to-follow system that reads a company’s financial statements, turns them into everyday health checks, and warns — one year ahead — if a company looks like it might get into serious financial trouble.

Field: Big Data Analytics & Finance
Discipline: Data Science · Machine Learning · Financial Risk Analytics
Deliverable: Data Pipeline, Predictive Model, Explainability Layer, Interactive Dashboard

1. Introduction

1.1 Project Background

Companies sometimes get into serious money trouble — they cannot pay their bills, they owe too much debt, or they keep losing money. This is called “financial distress.” Big investors, banks, and even the company’s own managers want to know about this kind of trouble as early as possible, so they can act before it becomes a real crisis, like a bankruptcy.

This project uses real company financial numbers from 50 companies (2023 to 2025) to build a simple system that reads a company’s financial statements and gives an early warning sign — like a weather forecast, but for a company’s financial health.

1.2 Problem Statement

Right now, many people only find out a company is in trouble after it is already too late — after the bad news is already public. What is missing is a simple tool that looks at a company’s numbers today and honestly says: “this company might be in trouble next year, and here is why.” This project tries to solve that problem, using the data that was given, while being upfront about how much (or how little) that data can really tell us.

1.3 Project Objectives

The project aims to:

  • Check the given data carefully for mistakes, missing numbers, and strange values before trusting it.
  • Turn raw financial numbers (like Revenue, Debt, Cash) into simple ratios that are easier to compare between companies.
  • Build a model that uses this year’s numbers to guess next year’s risk — not just repeat what we already know about this year.
  • Explain, in plain words, WHY a company is seen as risky — not just give a number with no reason.
  • Turn the model’s output into an easy 0–100 score anyone can understand.
  • Build a simple, interactive dashboard so a non-technical person can explore the results.
  • Be completely honest about the size of the dataset and what it can and cannot prove.

1.4 Project Scope

This project covers 50 companies across 3 years (2023, 2024, 2025), using financial statement data and a distress-event label file that was provided. It covers cleaning the data, building financial ratios, training and comparing 4 machine learning models, explaining the model’s decisions, building a risk score, and presenting everything on a dashboard.

This project does NOT cover: live/real-time data feeds, data from more than 50 companies, or any guarantee that the model works well outside of this specific small dataset. It is a demonstration project, not a live production system.

1.5 Project Significance

Even on a small scale, this project shows how a complete early-warning system could work in real life: from raw numbers, to a trained model, to a score a manager could actually read and act on. It also shows good practice — being honest about what the data can and cannot support, instead of over-promising results that a small dataset cannot back up.

2. Data & Information

2.1 Data Sources

Two data files were provided for this project:

  • 50-companies-financial.csv — financial statement numbers for 50 companies across 2023–2025.
  • distress_labels.csv — whether each company was marked as “in distress” in a given year, and what caused it.

2.2 Data Description

The financial data file has 149 rows (not a perfect 150, because one company is missing one year — explained in Section 2.4). It has four groups of information, shown below.

GroupWhat it tells usExample columns
Company InfoWhich company, which year, what industryCompany Name, Ticker, Industry, Year
Income StatementHow much money the company made or lostRevenue, Cost of Sales, Gross Profit, EBIT, Net Income
Balance SheetWhat the company owns and owesCash, Inventory, Total Assets, Total Debt, Total Equity
Cash Flow StatementHow cash actually moved in and outOperating Cash Flow, Capital Expenditure

The labels file has 150 rows and tells us, for each company and year, whether that company was marked as distressed (a value of 1) or healthy (a value of 0), what event caused the distress (for example, “Severe Debt Restructuring”), and the year that event actually happened.

2.3 Data Collection

Both files were supplied directly for this project as ready-made CSV (spreadsheet-style) files. No web-scraping or live API pulling was performed — all validation work in this project was about checking the quality of the given files, not about collecting new data.

2.4 Data Limitations

Before any modelling was done, both files were checked carefully. Here is what was found, explained simply:

  • FUBO (fuboTV) is missing its 2025 numbers. We left this blank — we did not make up a number.
  • GameStop (GME) has financial numbers but no distress label at all. We kept its numbers but marked its label as “unknown” — we did not guess.
  • SATS (EchoStar) has a distress label but no financial numbers, so it could not be used at all.
  • 19 rows show negative Total Equity (the company owes more than it owns). This is a real warning sign, not a data mistake, so we kept it.
  • 48 rows show negative EBIT (a real operating loss). Also kept, because it is a real financial signal.
  • A small number of rows (10 columns, a handful of rows each) have missing values. We left these blank instead of guessing a number.
Most important data problem found

Every single company shows “not distressed” for the year 2025 — even companies that were clearly struggling, like American Airlines, AMC, and BlackBerry. This is almost certainly because the label file had not yet recorded any 2025 events when it was built, not because every company suddenly became healthy. This finding directly shaped how the model was built (see Section 3.2.3).

3. Methodology

3.1 Overall Approach

The project follows a simple, step-by-step pipeline, like an assembly line: check the data, clean the data, combine the two files, build ratios, look for patterns, train and compare models, explain the model’s decisions, turn the results into a score, and finally show everything on a dashboard. Every step was written as its own small, readable piece of code, and every step was tested to make sure it actually works.

3.2 Data Preparation

3.2.1 Data Cleaning

Company names and ticker symbols were tidied up (removing extra spaces and stray punctuation). Numbers stored as text were safely converted into real numbers. No financial figures were changed, no rows were deleted, and no missing numbers were guessed or filled in — a rule followed throughout the whole project.

3.2.2 Data Transformation

The two files (financial numbers and distress labels) were joined together using the company’s ticker symbol and year, since ticker symbols are more reliable than company names (which are sometimes written slightly differently). After joining, every match and mismatch was reported and checked by hand, not just assumed to be correct.

3.2.3 Feature / Variable Preparation

Raw dollar figures (like Revenue or Total Debt) are hard to compare between a huge company and a small one. So, raw numbers were turned into ratios — simple, fair comparisons like “Current Ratio” or “Debt-to-Equity” (fully explained in Section 3.4).

The project also needed a proper “early warning” target: using this year’s numbers to predict NEXT year’s distress, instead of just repeating what we already know about this year. But a serious problem was found: since every company shows “not distressed” for 2025 (see Section 2.4), the pairing of “2024 data predicting 2025” could not be trusted — a model trained on it would just learn to always say “safe”, which teaches us nothing. Only the pairing of “2023 data predicting 2024” could be trusted. This left just 49 usable rows, with 13 of them truly becoming distressed the following year.

It was also discovered that “year-over-year change” features (like “did Revenue grow this year?”) cannot be worked out for 2023, because there is no 2022 data to compare it to — and 2023 is our only trustworthy training year. So the final model only uses a single year’s snapshot ratios, not trend changes. Trend changes are still calculated and shown on the dashboard for 2024 and 2025, just not used to train the model.

3.3 Analytical Methods

Four machine learning models were built and fairly compared: Logistic Regression (a simple, easy-to-explain method), Decision Tree, Random Forest, and XGBoost (two more advanced “tree-based” methods). Because there were only 49 trustworthy rows, a single train/test split would not be reliable — it could look artificially good or bad purely by chance. Instead, Stratified 5-Fold Cross-Validation was used: the 49 rows were split into 5 balanced groups, the model was trained on 4 groups and tested on the 1 left out, five times over, so every row gets tested exactly once. The five results were then averaged for a fairer picture.

SHAP (a well-known explainability method) was then used on the best model to explain, for any single company, which financial ratios pushed its risk score up or down, and by how much.

3.4 Metrics & Calculations

The following ratios were calculated for every company, every year. All formulas return a blank value (instead of a fake huge number) whenever a safe division is not possible, such as dividing by zero.

Liquidity — can the company pay its short-term bills?

  • Current Ratio = Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities
  • Quick Ratio = (Current Assets − Inventory) ÷ Current Liabilities
  • Cash Ratio = Cash & Cash Equivalents ÷ Current Liabilities

Profitability — is the company making money?

  • Net Profit Margin = Net Income ÷ Revenue
  • EBIT Margin = EBIT ÷ Revenue
  • Return on Assets (ROA) = Net Income ÷ Total Assets
  • Return on Equity (ROE) = Net Income ÷ Total Equity (flagged as unreliable when Equity is negative)

Leverage — how much debt does the company carry?

  • Debt-to-Equity = Total Debt ÷ Total Equity
  • Debt Ratio = Total Debt ÷ Total Assets
  • Interest Coverage = EBIT ÷ Interest Expense

Efficiency — how well does the company use what it owns?

  • Asset Turnover = Revenue ÷ Total Assets
  • Inventory Turnover = Cost of Sales ÷ Average Inventory
  • Receivables Turnover = Revenue ÷ Average Accounts Receivable

Cash Flow Risk — is cash actually coming in?

  • Operating Cash Flow Ratio = Operating Cash Flow ÷ Current Liabilities
  • Cash Flow to Debt = Operating Cash Flow ÷ Total Debt
  • Free Cash Flow = Operating Cash Flow − Capital Expenditure

3.5 Assumptions

  • It is assumed that the financial figures provided are accurate as reported by each company (this project does not attempt to re-audit the original company filings).
  • It is assumed that a company’s own past ratios are a reasonable guide to its near-future risk, which is a standard assumption in financial analysis.
  • It is assumed that the 2025 “not distressed” labels are incomplete rather than genuinely true for every company (see Section 2.4), and the modelling approach was adjusted accordingly.
  • Rule-based alert thresholds (e.g., “Current Ratio below 1”) are treated as common, adjustable rules of thumb, not as fixed laws of accounting.

4. Solution / System Design

4.1 Solution Overview

The finished solution is a small pipeline of Python programs plus a dashboard. Each program does one clear job — cleaning, merging, ratio-building, model training, explaining, scoring, or recommending — and each one can be run and checked on its own. The final output is a single table with every company, every year, its risk score, its risk category, its top risk drivers, and simple management recommendations — all displayed through the dashboard.

4.2 System Architecture

The project is organised into clear folders, each with one job:

FolderPurpose
data/raw/The original files, untouched
data/processed/Cleaned, merged, ratio, and final scored data
src/All the Python code (the “engine” of the project)
models/The saved, trained machine learning models
dashboard/The interactive Streamlit application (6 pages), plus a static HTML snapshot
reports/Written reports, charts, and explainability outputs
tests/Automatic checks that confirm the pipeline still works correctly

4.3 Data Flow

Data moves through the system in one direction, step by step, like a factory line:

  • 1. Raw files (financial data + labels) are loaded.
  • 2. Data cleaning fixes text formatting only — no numbers are changed.
  • 3. The two files are merged (joined) using ticker + year.
  • 4. Financial ratios are calculated from the merged data.
  • 5. Trend features and the next-year target are added.
  • 6. Models are trained and compared using cross-validation.
  • 7. The best model produces a probability score for every company-year.
  • 8. SHAP explains each score; the probability becomes a 0–100 risk score; alerts and recommendations are generated.
  • 9. Everything lands in one final table, which powers the dashboard.

4.4 Technology Stack

PurposeTool(s) used
Programming languagePython 3
Data handlingpandas, numpy
Chartsmatplotlib, seaborn, plotly, Chart.js (static HTML)
Machine learningscikit-learn, XGBoost
ExplainabilitySHAP

4.5 Dashboard / Interface Design

The dashboard has six pages, built so a non-technical manager could use it without any training: Executive Overview, Company Risk Monitor, Financial Health, Why Is This Company Risky?, Early-Warning Monitor, and Industry Risk. It is available in two forms: a live Streamlit app, and a self-contained static HTML file with the same data and working filters/search, viewable in any browser with no installation. Screenshots are provided in Appendix 10.5.

5. Analysis & Results

5.1 Descriptive Analysis

Out of 149 usable company-year records, 39 are labelled as distressed at some point and 111 as healthy — meaning roughly 1 in 4 records show a company in some form of financial trouble. This comes from 50 companies across 38 different industries, so most industries only have one to three companies represented.

5.2 Trend Analysis

Looking at the numbers over time, distressed companies show a clearly different pattern from healthy ones. Distressed companies tend to carry a higher and often rising Debt Ratio, while healthy companies tend to keep theirs stable or falling.

5.3 Key Findings

5.3.1 Finding 1 — Cash and profit ratios matter more than raw debt

The model’s own explanation (SHAP) shows that “Cash Flow to Net Income” (does reported profit turn into real cash?), Net Profit Margin, and Return on Assets were the strongest signals of risk — even stronger than the debt-related ratios most people expect to matter most.

5.3.2 Finding 2 — A small group of companies stand out as clearly high-risk

In the most recent year of data (2025), 10 companies fall into the “Critical Risk” category and 3 into “High Risk”, out of 49 companies with a usable score. These companies share common warning signs: negative cash flow, weak interest coverage, and negative profit.

RankCompanyIndustryRisk Score (0–100)

5.3.3 Finding 3 — The dataset is too small to fully trust the model’s precision

The model that performed best overall — XGBoost — correctly caught about 77 out of every 100 companies that actually became distressed the following year (a Recall of 0.767), and separated risky from safe companies well (a ROC-AUC of 0.911). These are respectable numbers, but they come from only 49 rows and 13 real distress cases, so the exact numbers should be read as a promising direction, not a proven, stable result.

XGBoost was chosen as the main model because catching real distress cases (Recall) was decided to be more important than raw accuracy — missing a company that is about to fail is a worse mistake than double-checking one that turns out fine.

5.5 Business Impact

For a manager or investor, this system means they can look up any company and instantly see: its risk score, WHY it is risky (in plain financial terms), and a suggested next action — instead of manually reading through financial statements line by line. Even on a small dataset, this shows how such a system could save real time and catch problems earlier once it is trained on a much larger set of companies.

6. Recommendations

6.1 Key Recommendations

  • Treat this project’s risk scores as a starting point for further investigation, not a final answer — always check the company’s actual financial statements before making any real decision.
  • Focus first on the small group of “Critical Risk” companies shown in Section 5.3.2 — they show the clearest, most consistent warning signs across multiple ratios at once.
  • Use the “Why Is This Company Risky?” dashboard page to understand WHICH specific ratio is driving a company’s risk score before deciding what action to take.

6.2 Short-Term Actions

  • Review the Critical and High Risk companies identified in this report and compare them against their most recent public financial filings, since our data only goes up to 2025.
  • For any company flagged with a cash flow warning (negative Operating Cash Flow), prioritise checking its ability to pay short-term bills before anything else.
  • Share this report and dashboard with relevant finance or risk teams as an early, low-cost screening tool — not as a replacement for a full credit review.

6.3 Long-Term Actions

  • Grow the dataset to include many more companies and many more years, so the model can be trained and tested properly (see Section 7.4).
  • Set up a process to keep the distress labels updated every year, so future “predict next year” comparisons are trustworthy.
  • Once enough data is available, consider re-testing whether the model still performs well on companies and industries it has never seen before.

7. Limitations & Future Improvements

This section is written to be direct and honest. A good project is judged not only by its results, but by how clearly it explains what those results do NOT prove.

7.1 Project Limitations

  • The project covers only 50 companies over 3 years — a small slice of the real corporate world.
  • The dashboard and model reflect a snapshot in time; they are not connected to any live, constantly updating data feed.

7.2 Data Limitations

  • Only 49 rows could be trusted for training and testing the early-warning model, with just 13 of them being real distress cases — a very small number for machine learning.
  • Every company shows “not distressed” for 2025, most likely because the label file had not caught up with 2025 events yet — not because every company became safe.
  • Some rows do not perfectly satisfy the basic accounting rule that Assets = Liabilities + Equity, most likely due to extra balance-sheet items not included in this dataset.
  • Most industries only have 1 to 3 companies, so industry-level comparisons should be read as illustrative, not statistically solid.

7.3 Methodological Limitations

  • With only 49 training rows split into 5 cross-validation groups, each group has roughly 10 rows — individual group results can swing a lot just by chance.
  • Trend features (like “did Revenue grow this year?”) could not be used to train the model at all, because the only trustworthy training year (2023) has no prior year to compare against.
  • Some of the model’s top risk signals closely match the wording used in the original distress event descriptions. This means the model is partly re-confirming the same criteria a human used to write the label, rather than discovering a completely hidden pattern.
  • The 0–100 Risk Score is an internal, simplified score for this project only. It is explicitly NOT an official credit rating and should never be used as one.

7.4 Future Improvements

  • Collect more years of history (ideally 5 or more years, for many more companies) so a proper time-based train/validate/test split becomes possible.
  • Add more companies within each industry, so industry comparisons become statistically meaningful instead of just descriptive.
  • Test the model using several different random seeds to check how stable its results really are.
  • Bring in an outside, larger, well-known dataset (such as a public historical bankruptcy dataset) to check whether the model still works well outside of these exact 50 companies.
  • If new companies (for example, TNB) become available in the same data format, add them as a real-world featured case study.

8. Conclusion

8.1 Project Summary

This project set out to build a simple early-warning system for company financial distress. It moved through every honest step of a real data science project: checking the data carefully, cleaning it without guessing, building meaningful financial ratios, discovering and documenting a real problem in the label data, training and comparing four models the right way for a small dataset, explaining every prediction, and packaging everything into an easy-to-use dashboard.

8.2 Key Outcomes

  • A fully working, tested, and reproducible data pipeline, from raw files to final risk scores.
  • A best-performing model (XGBoost) that correctly catches about 77% of real distress cases in cross-validation testing.
  • A working explainability layer (SHAP) that shows the specific reasons behind every company’s risk score.
  • A complete, 6-page dashboard, available both live (Streamlit) and as an offline, self-contained HTML file.
  • An honestly documented set of limitations, so nobody mistakes this small demonstration for a certified financial product.

8.3 Final Remarks

The biggest lesson from this project is that good data science is not just about getting a high accuracy number — it is about knowing exactly how much to trust your own results, and saying so clearly. With a bigger dataset, the same pipeline built here could become a genuinely useful early-warning tool. For now, it stands as a complete, honest, and working demonstration of how such a tool could be built the right way.

10.3 Additional Results (Charts & Tables)

10.4 Code / Technical Details

The complete project source code is provided as a separate folder alongside this report. It contains 11 Python scripts, each handling one clear step of the pipeline, totalling approximately 1,127 lines of commented code.

ScriptWhat it does
data_validation.pyChecks the raw data for problems (missing values, duplicates, formula mismatches) without changing anything.
data_cleaning.pyFixes text formatting only (names, tickers); never guesses missing numbers.
merge_data.pyJoins the financial data and the distress labels using Ticker and Year.
financial_ratios.pyCalculates all liquidity, profitability, leverage, efficiency, and cash-flow ratios safely.
feature_engineering.pyBuilds year-over-year trend features and the shifted “next year” target.
eda.pyGenerates all comparison and trend charts.
train.pyTrains and cross-validates all four machine learning models.
threshold_optimization.pyTests different decision thresholds and reports the trade-offs.
explainability.pyRuns SHAP to explain the model’s predictions, globally and per company.
risk_scoring.pyConverts model probabilities into the 0–100 Risk Score and generates alerts.
recommendations.pyGenerates evidence-based management recommendations for each company.

Example — the safe-division function used throughout the ratio calculations, so that dividing by zero never produces a broken or misleading number:

def _safe_divide(numerator, denominator):
    """Divide two columns, but return a blank value (NaN)
    instead of infinity when the denominator is 0 or missing."""
    denominator = denominator.replace(0, np.nan)
    return numerator / denominator

Example — the rule that decides which financial year pairs can be trusted to build the early-warning target:

def build_next_year_target(df):
    """For every company-year row (Year = T), look up that SAME
    company's Distress Status at Year = T+1. If Year T+1 is not in
    our data, the target is left blank (NaN) instead of guessed."""
